AI assistance was used to prepare this post and its teaching example. The executable cases below were run locally. This code is independent of the product's implementation and does not call its service. Define what a passing result means Here, canContinue means the selected files match the local preflight rules, so the UI can let the user review the request. It does not authorize an upload, confirm available credits, or start generation. The example policy uses JPEG/PNG, a 10 MiB limit per file, and an exact photo count. These are illustrative policy values , not claims about any particular service's supported formats or upload limits. In an integration, obtain the policy from an authorized, versioned source and match it to the backend's rules. Keep these checks separate: Missing or malformed template requirements: block continuation and explain what is unavailable. Incorrect file count: tell the user the count for the currently selected template. Unknown or unsupported MIME metadata: ask for a supported file rather than silently treating it as an image. Empty or oversized file: identify the affected selection. A pure validator Save this as dev-photo-selection.mjs : export function validateSelection ( template , files ) { const validTemplate = template && Number . isInteger ( template . requiredPhotos ) && template . requiredPhotos > 0 && Number . isFinite ( template . maxBytes ) && template . maxBytes > 0 && Array . isArray ( template . allowedTypes ) && template . allowedTypes . length > 0 && template . allowedTypes . every ( type => typeof type === ' string ' && type . length > 0 ); if ( ! validTemplate ) { return { canContinue : false , errors : [ ' Template requirements unavailable. ' ] }; } if ( ! Array . isArray ( files )) { return { canContinue : false , errors : [ ' Choose your photos again. ' ] }; } const errors = []; if ( files . length !== template . requiredPhotos ) { errors . push ( `Choose exactly ${ template . requiredPhotos } photo(s).` ); } files . forEach (( file , index ) => { if ( ! file || ! template . allowedTypes . includes ( file . type )) { errors . push ( `Photo ${ index + 1 } : unsupported or unknown file type.` ); } if ( ! file || ! Number . isFinite ( file . size ) || file . size <= 0 || file . size > template . maxBytes ) { errors . push ( `Photo ${ index + 1 } : file size is outside the allowed range.` ); } }); return { canContinue : errors . length === 0 , errors }; } The function accepts an ordinary array. In a browser, convert the chosen FileList with Array.from(input.files) before calling it. The test objects below contain only type and size ; the function does not read file bytes. An invalid selection can produce multiple useful errors. For example, switching from a two-photo template to a one-photo template must invalidate a two-file selection even if both files meet the type and size rules. No file is silently discarded to make the count pass. Exercise the boundaries Save this next to the module as dev-photo-selection.test.mjs : import assert from ' node:assert/strict ' ; import { validateSelection } from ' ./dev-photo-selection.mjs ' ; const one = { requiredPhotos : 1 , allowedTypes : [ ' image/jpeg ' , ' image/png ' ], maxBytes : 10 * 1024 * 1024 }; const two = { ... one , requiredPhotos : 2 }; const photo = { type : ' image/jpeg ' , size : 2048 }; const cases = [ [ ' one photo ' , one , [ photo ], true ], [ ' two photos ' , two , [ photo , { ... photo }], true ], [ ' missing photo ' , two , [ photo ], false ], [ ' extra photo after switching template ' , one , [ photo , photo ], false ], [ ' empty selection ' , one , [], false ], [ ' empty file ' , one , [{ ... photo , size : 0 }], false ], [ ' exact byte limit ' , one , [{ ... photo , size : one . maxBytes }], true ], [ ' one byte over limit ' , one , [{ ... photo , size : one . maxBytes + 1 }], false ], [ ' wrong MIME ' , one , [{ ... photo , type : ' video/mp4 ' }], false ], [ ' unknown MIME ' , one , [{ ... photo , type : '' }], false ], [ ' invalid size ' , one , [{ ... photo , size : Infinity }], false ], [ ' missing metadata ' , null , [ photo ], false ], [ ' invalid count metadata ' , { ... one , requiredPhotos : 0 }, [ photo ], false ], [ ' empty MIME policy ' , { ... one , allowedTypes : [] }, [ photo ], false ], [ ' malformed file list ' , one , null , false ], [ ' malformed file entry ' , one , [ null ], false ] ]; const before = JSON . stringify ({ one , two , photo }); for ( const [ name , template , files , expected ] of cases ) { const result = validateSelection ( template , files ); assert . equal ( result . canContinue , expected , name ); assert . equal ( result . errors . length === 0 , expected , name + ' error messages ' ); } assert . equal ( JSON . stringify ({ one , two , photo }), before , ' inputs preserved ' ); console . log ( ` ${ cases . length } cases passed; inputs preserved. No network or uploads.` ); Run: node dev-photo-selection.test.mjs The local result was: 16 cases passed; inputs preserved. No network or uploads. The byte-limit boundary is intentional: a file at the limit passes; one byte above it fails. Empty metadata also fails explicitly. It does not become a one-photo template through a default value. Revalidate when the template changes Run the validator on both file selection and template changes. If your UI loads template requirements asynchronously, keep continuation disabled while the new requirements are unavailable. Associate the response with the selected template ID and version so an older response cannot replace the current requirements. Show the returned messages near the file input. Keep an explicit next step for reviewing the selected template and any current credit cost. Do not trigger a paid generation request just because local validation passed. Keep server validation authoritative A browser file's reported type is a preflight hint, not proof of its contents. The server still needs to enforce its size and count limits, inspect and decode the received files, verify ownership and authorization, and validate the template and charging rules. The browser's accept attribute helps selection; it does not replace those checks. The example also says nothing about portrait suitability, consent, image dimensions, pose, or the generated video's quality. Add those checks where your actual workflow requires them, with clear messages and appropriate review steps. References: MDN's file input documentation and Using files from web applications .

title: GEO Score Explained: What It Measures and How to Fix It
author: GrowGanic
summary: A GEO score grades how often AI answer engines quote your pages for the questions your content should own, and it moves only when you fix the content gaps behind it. It is not a ranking, not a traffic forecast, and not a vanity metric you can inflate with volume. Treat it as a diagnostic you act on by repairing the passages that fail extraction, and the number follows the work. What the Number Actually Grades A GEO score is a citation-frequency estimate: it approximates how often AI answer surfaces pull a passage from your page when someone asks a question your topic covers. It is a measure of extractability and visibility inside generated answers, not a measure of Google rankings, backlinks, or domain strength. Adjacent concepts get confused here constantly. Generative engine optimization, usually shortened to generative engine optimization , is the discipline of making content quotable by answer engines. The score is the readout of how well a given page or site performs inside that discipline. It serves anyone who depends on being mentioned when a buyer asks an assistant a question, which increasingly means solo founders and small teams competing against brands with content departments. What it is not matters just as much. A rising score does not guarantee traffic; many AI answers cite a source without sending a click. A flat score does not mean your content is bad, only that it is not being selected for extraction. And a high score on one page never transfers to another, because extraction is judged per passage, per question, per query fan-out. Signals Worth Checking Before You Rewrite Anything Before you touch a draft, look at what the score is actually reacting to. These are the criteria that separate a page built for citations from a page that only reads well to a human. The broader generative engine framework explains why each one matters, but the checklist below is what you inspect. Signal What to inspect Why it decides citations Answer placement Does the first sentence after the heading answer the question? Extractors grab the cleanest lead, not the most thorough page Statistic provenance Is every number tied to a named source with a date? Unsourced figures get dropped when the model assembles an answer Entity clarity Is the subject named the same way everywhere on the page? Ambiguous naming splits the entity the model is trying to match Section self-containment Can a section be quoted with no surrounding context? Chunks get pulled out of order, so each must stand alone Freshness stamps Is there a visible date on reviewed or updated content? Stale passages lose to fresher ones covering the same query Source-of-record links Do claims link to the exact page carrying the fact? Models favor passages whose supporting evidence is checkable None of these are abstract. You can open the page and see all six in a few minutes. If more than two fail, the score is describing a real defect, not noise. Fixing the Gaps a Score Exposes Each fix below targets a specific extraction failure. They run in sequence, because each one changes what the next step has to work with. Rewrite the opening of every section so the first sentence answers the heading's question directly, then support it. Buried answers are the single most common reason a competent page never gets quoted. Replace every unsourced statistic with a cited one, or delete the number. A value is only as quotable as the source behind it. Our own rule is blunt: statistics come from sources we checked, each with its check date, and no source means no statistic. Standardize how you name the subject across the page, the headings, and the internal links. One name, used consistently, gives the model a clean entity to attach the passage to. Split long argumentative sections into passages that survive being quoted alone. If a paragraph only makes sense after the paragraph above it, an extractor will skip both. Schedule the pass instead of doing it once. Ranking and citation behavior shift, so the same page needs re-reading against a fresh view of what is currently winning the answer for your query. That is the mechanical version of the work, and it is genuinely repetitive. It is also the reason we built the system we run for this. GrowGanic reads the pages currently ranking on page one, writes for the intent they show, and publishes on a cadence, which is the only way this holds up over months rather than a weekend. Reading the Signals That Decide Your Next Move You are staring at a score that has not moved, and you have two options: keep rewriting, or rebuild the page from scratch. Which one is right depends on signals you can check today. If the page ranks on Google for the query but AI answers cite competitors instead, the problem is extractability, and rewriting is the correct and cheaper move. If the page does not rank at all for the underlying query, the problem is upstream and no amount of passage-tightening will help. If the score is flat across an entire topic cluster while one competitor's pages get quoted repeatedly, you are losing a category, not a page, and you should check whether your sections answer the same fan-out questions the answers cover. There is a fourth case worth naming: a page that ranks, gets quoted, and still shows no score improvement. That usually means the query is being answered from a knowledge source the model treats as authoritative, and your realistic goal shifts from being the primary answer to being the corroborating one. Pick your move based on which of these four states you are in. Rewriting a page that should be rebuilt wastes weeks. Where Practitioners Go Wrong Treating the score as a target rather than a readout is the first trap. People optimize the number, add the same phrase more times, and the underlying page is no more quotable than before. The score was never the thing changing; it was the symptom. Confusing it with a Google ranking is the second. A page can rank third and never appear in an AI answer, because the two systems reward different things. One rewards relevance and authority across a results page; the other rewards clean, sourced, self-contained passages that survive extraction. Google's own Search Console describes its tools as a way to measure Search traffic and performance and fix issues in Google Search, and that framing is the tell: it measures Search behavior, not answer-engine citation behavior. Reading one as a proxy for the other leads people to fix the wrong problem. Sourcing is where the fastest corrections live. A claim with no linked origin reads as an opinion, and opinions get skipped when a model is assembling a fact-based answer. Attach the source or cut the number. The habit that costs the most time is the one-off audit. A single pass produces a snapshot, and snapshots go stale the moment the answer format shifts. What holds is a system that publishes, measures, and re-checks on a schedule, so the fixes keep landing without a person re-running the whole exercise by hand. Frequently Asked Questions Before you dig further, the fastest way to watch a score move is to start publishing on a plan that fits your volume. See the current numbers on the GrowGanic pricing page and pick the tier that matches how fast you want to run the pass. What is a GEO score? A GEO score is an estimate of how often AI answer engines quote your pages for the questions your content should own. It reflects extractability, meaning whether your passages are clean, sourced and self-contained enough for a model to lift them into an answer. It is separate from your Google ranking, your backlink profile and your domain strength. Improving it means fixing the content behind the number, never inflating the number itself. How do I raise a GEO score? You raise it by repairing the specific passages that fail extraction, not by publishing more pages. Front-load the answer in the first sentence of each section, tie every statistic to a named source with a check date, name your subject consistently across the page, and split long arguments into passages that survive being quoted alone. Then republish, re-measure, and compare. If the same page still is not cited after a full rewrite, the problem is usually the topic itself, not the wording. Does a higher GEO score mean more traffic? Not automatically. AI answers frequently cite a source without generating a click, so a rising score means you are being named more often in generated answers, not that visits will climb in step. The value shows up in brand mentions, corroboration and trust at the point a buyer is deciding. Track it next to your Google rankings and organic sessions rather than instead of them, and judge it on whether the right questions start routing through your content. Stop writing articles. Start shipping them.

title: Open-Weights Day Is November 4: Redo Your Own-vs-Rent Math (Most of You Will Still Rent)
author: T.M. Gunderson
summary: The first frontier-class download has a date Moonshot AI says the full weights of Kimi K3.1 Pro — its flagship, a 3T-class model with a one-million-token context window — ship by November 4. Until then the model runs through the company's apps and API only; after that, in principle, you can run it on hardware you control. The quality claim is not vendor hype alone. Artificial Analysis, which benchmarks models independently, scores K3.1 Pro at 55 on its Intelligence Index — fourth among all models it tracks, three points behind the leader (Claude Opus 5.5 at 58), one point behind Claude Sonnet 5.5, and nine points above the best open-weights model available today. It lists at $2 per million input tokens and $10 out — the same price as Sonnet 5.5, and a third cheaper than its own predecessor, Kimi K3. That last detail is why this is a business story rather than a benchmark story. For the first time, "download a frontier-class model and run it yourself" is a question with a date on it. Which makes own-vs-rent a recheckable question — not a stance you adopted once and forgot. A downloadable model is not a free model Open weights mean you get the recipe, not the meal. Once the weights are in hand, every cost the vendor was absorbing becomes yours: Hardware. A 2.8-trillion-parameter model does not run on the office laptop. It needs serious GPUs — bought, or rented by the hour. Operations. Someone installs it, keeps it running, restarts it when it falls over, and upgrades it when a better version ships. That someone is you, or a contractor you pay. Security and hygiene. The server is now your server — patching, access control, backups. A model with access to your business data is an attack surface like any other. When you rent AI, you are borrowing a vendor's ops team amortized across thousands of customers. That is the actual product. The model weights were never the expensive part. The honest checklist: when self-hosting still does not make sense Run down this list before you get excited about November 4: No compliance driver. If no regulator, contract, or client requires your data to stay on your infrastructure, you would be self-hosting to save money that probably is not there. Unpredictable volume. Self-hosting pays for peak capacity whether or not the peak shows up. Bursty, occasional use is exactly what APIs were built for. No ops person. Not "you are handy with computers" — an actual human accountable for uptime. If the honest answer is "it would be me, at night," that is the answer. Most small businesses check all three boxes. That is not a failure — it is the correct result, and knowing it is the point of the exercise. The three signals it is time to reprice Self-hosting earns a fresh look when any of these is true: Regulated or confidential data. Healthcare, legal, finance, or client contracts that demand data residency. Here the comparison is not price — it is what a vendor's breach clause costs you versus keeping the data inside in the first place. Predictable high volume. Steady, heavy, round-the-clock token use flattens your unit cost and makes capacity planning real. Volume you can forecast is capacity you can buy efficiently. Renegotiation leverage. A tested, working fallback is the only thing that makes a vendor's renewal desk polite. Even if you never switch, the credible ability to switch reprices the contract you are already in — which matters in a market where frontier AI is being financed on expectations and the bill eventually lands somewhere. The 30-minute math One sitting, three lines: What you spend now. Annual AI spend: subscriptions plus API usage. The real number, from the card statement, not the guess. What self-hosting would cost. Hourly GPU rental for a model of this class, sized to your actual volume for the hours you would actually use it — plus a monthly ops line even if the ops person is you, because your time is not free either. The difference. If line two is not clearly smaller — not marginally, clearly — keep renting. The output is a number, not a decision. Most businesses run this and land on rent. The value is that the next time a vendor raises prices or a contract comes up for renewal, you are arguing from a number instead of a feeling. What to actually do on November 4 Three things, in order: Read the license. It was not published at announcement, and "open weights" is a marketing phrase until it is. The license decides whether commercial use, hosting for clients, and productization are allowed — and those terms can change the math on their own. Recheck your trigger list. No compliance driver, no predictable volume, no renewal on the table? Note the date and move on. The math does not expire, but it deserves a quarterly recheck — this category re-prices faster than most software you buy. If a signal applies, price it. One evening, the three lines, done. Honest boundaries The weights are not in hand yet. "By November 4" is a promise, and ship dates in this industry have slipped before. Nothing here requires the download to exist for the math to be worth having. Hold the benchmark numbers loosely. The Artificial Analysis index is independent; Moonshot's own comparison tables are vendor-run and should be read as direction, not measurement. Renting is not the same as ignoring. The rent lane still needs its own discipline — a quarterly review of what you pay and which tier you are on. Cheap self-hosting math does not excuse a lazy rental bill. This is a recheck, not a switch. If you finish this post more certain you should rent than when you started, it did its job. Tonight's version Write the three lines: what you spend, what self-hosting would cost, the difference. Thirty minutes. Mark November 4 on the calendar to read the license. That is the whole assignment — most of you will still rent, but now you will know why, and you will have the number to prove it. Want the worksheets? The Boring Automation Pack includes the spend-audit and quarterly-review worksheets — the rent-lane discipline that keeps this math honest between rechecks.

title: Vibe Coding Security: 8 Holes in Almost Every AI-Built App
author: Muhammad Moiz
summary: Originally published at muhammadmoiz.dev . Vibe coding security comes down to one problem: AI app builders are very good at making features work and much less careful about who is allowed to use them. The same handful of holes turn up again and again in AI-built apps, and most of them are about access control, leaked keys and trusting the browser. Below are the 8 that come up most often, how to check for each one in an afternoon, and what to do when you find them. This is written for founders who built with Lovable, Bolt, Replit, Cursor or v0, and for developers who just inherited one of those projects. Is Lovable safe? Why AI-built apps share the same weaknesses The tools themselves are not the problem. The problem is the default architecture they produce. Most AI builders generate a React frontend that talks directly to a backend-as-a-service such as Supabase or Firebase. There is often no server of your own in between. That means the browser is the only place where "rules" live, unless someone deliberately writes them into the database. This is not a theory. CVE-2025-48757, published on 30 May 2025, describes insufficient Row Level Security in sites generated by Lovable up to 15 April 2025, which let unauthenticated attackers read or write arbitrary tables. The CVE record gives it a CVSS 3.1 base score of 9.3 (critical). Lovable disputes the entry, and the record notes their position that each customer is responsible for protecting their own app's data. That dispute is the key lesson for any founder: whoever's fault it is, your users' data is your responsibility. The AI tool will not be the one emailing your customers about a breach. The 8 vibe coding security holes 1. Row Level Security is missing or does nothing With Supabase, your publishable (anon) key ships inside the frontend. That is by design. Supabase's own docs say requests made with it are limited to whatever Row Level Security allows. So RLS is the actual lock on your data. The common failures: RLS is turned off on one or more tables in the public schema. RLS is on, but a policy like using (true) lets everyone read everything. Policies check that a user is logged in, but not that the row belongs to them. A safer pattern for a table where each user owns their rows looks like this: alter table invoices enable row level security ; create policy "owners read their invoices" on invoices for select to authenticated using (( select auth . uid ()) is not null and ( select auth . uid ()) = owner_id ); Supabase recommends the explicit is not null check because auth.uid() returns null for anonymous requests, and wrapping it in select lets Postgres evaluate it once per query instead of once per row. I covered this hole in depth in Supabase RLS explained . 2. Secret keys shipped to the browser The Supabase secret key (formerly the service_role key) bypasses every RLS policy. It belongs on a server, in an Edge Function or in a scheduled job, never in frontend code, never in Git. A common way it ends up in client code: an AI assistant "fixes" a permissions error by swapping the publishable key for the secret one. The same mistake happens with environment variables. In Next.js, any variable prefixed with NEXT_PUBLIC_ is inlined into the JavaScript bundle at build time, so anyone can read it in their browser's dev tools. Other build tools have similar public prefixes. If a payment provider secret, OpenAI key or database password has a public prefix, treat it as leaked: rotate it, then move the call that needs it to the server. Quick check: open your live site, open dev tools, search the loaded JavaScript for sb_secret_ , service_role and the start of any secret key from your payment or AI provider. 3. Security rules that only exist in the UI Hiding the "Delete" button for non-admins is not security. Neither is a redirect on the admin page. Anyone can call your API, your Supabase tables or your server functions directly with a tool like curl. The Next.js docs make this point clearly for Server Actions: an exported action can be called with a direct POST request, so the page-level login check does not protect it. Each action needs its own check. ' use server ' import { getSession } from ' @/lib/session ' import { db } from ' @/lib/db ' export async function archiveProject ( projectId : string ) { const session = await getSession () if ( ! session ) throw new Error ( ' Not signed in ' ) const project = await db . project . findFirst ({ where : { id : projectId , ownerId : session . userId }, }) if ( ! project ) throw new Error ( ' Not found ' ) await db . project . update ({ where : { id : project . id }, data : { archived : true } }) return { ok : true } } 4. Trusting IDs sent from the client (IDOR) This is the cousin of hole 3. The user is logged in, but the app takes an ID from the URL or request body and loads that record without asking whether it belongs to them. Change /orders/1041 to /orders/1042 and you see a stranger's order. The OWASP name for this is Insecure Direct Object Reference. The fix is always the same: look up the record using both the ID and the current user (as in the example above), or let RLS enforce ownership in the database. 5. Admin flags and roles the user can edit AI-generated schemas often put role or is_admin on the same profiles table that users are allowed to update. If the update policy covers the whole row, any user can promote themselves to admin with one request. Another variant reads a role from local storage or a query string, which the Next.js docs specifically call out as untrusted input. Keep roles in a table users cannot write to, or restrict updates to specific columns, and verify the role on the server every time. 6. File storage that is more public than you think Uploaded invoices, ID photos and contracts often end up in a public bucket because that made the images load during development. In Supabase, objects in a public bucket can be read by anyone who has the URL, with no policy needed. Supabase does block uploads until you add policies on storage.objects , so AI tools sometimes add a very broad policy to make uploads work. Use private buckets for anything personal, generate signed URLs when a user needs to view a file, and scope storage policies to a folder per user. 7. No rate limits on expensive actions Supabase Auth applies rate limits to its own sign-in, sign-up and email endpoints. Your custom functions are a different story. A contact form that sends email, an endpoint that calls an AI model, or a function that writes to the database can be hit thousands of times by a script. The result is a surprise bill, a blacklisted email domain or a flooded database. The Next.js data security guide recommends rate limiting exactly these kinds of operations. Add per-IP and per-user limits to anything that costs money or sends messages, and set spending caps on your AI provider account. 8. Returning far more data than the screen needs A select * that sends the full user record to the browser, including email, phone, internal notes or a password reset token, is a leak even if the UI only shows the name. Anything in a network response is visible to the user who received it. Select only the columns the page needs. In Next.js, the docs recommend a server-only data layer that returns small, safe objects rather than raw database rows. Photo: Arnold Francisca on Unsplash Vibe coding best practices: a one-afternoon security checklist You can work through this list yourself before paying anyone. Each line is a yes/no question. Check How to test it Red flag RLS on every table Check each table's RLS status in the Supabase dashboard Any exposed table with RLS off Policies scoped to owner Read each policy's using clause true , or no auth.uid() reference No secrets in the bundle Search the live site's JS in dev tools sb_secret_ , service_role , any secret key Server checks on every action Call an endpoint with curl while logged out It succeeds Ownership checks Change an ID in the URL while logged in You see another user's data Roles protected Try updating your own role column via the API It works Private storage Open a document URL in a private window It loads Rate limits Submit a form 50 times quickly Every request succeeds Minimal responses Inspect network responses on profile pages Fields the UI never shows .env files out of Git Check your repo history A committed .env Test with a second account: Most of these holes only show up when you are logged in as one user and try to reach another user's data. Create two test accounts and try to read, edit and delete each other's records. If you can, so can anyone. What to do when you find a hole Rotate anything leaked first. A key that was ever in a public bundle or repository is compromised, even if you remove it now. Lock down the database. Enable RLS everywhere, then add the narrowest policies that keep the app working. Supabase's docs suggest testing allowed and denied operations for both the anon and authenticated roles. Move privileged calls to the server. Payments, emails, AI calls and admin operations belong in server routes or Edge Functions. Check your logs. Look for unusual reads or writes before the fix, in case you need to notify users. Stop the AI from undoing it. When you prompt for new features, tell the tool explicitly not to change policies or swap keys, and review every diff that touches auth or the database. What this means for founders and app owners An AI builder can get you to a working demo in days, and that is genuinely valuable. But "it works" and "it is safe to put real customer data in" are separate milestones. If you are about to take payments, store personal data, onboard a business client or raise money, a security review is part of shipping, not an extra. If the checklist turned up red flags, or you are not sure how to read the results, a production audit gives you a prioritised list of what is exposed and how to fix it. If you would rather hand the whole thing over, I also take AI-built apps to production , keeping what works and rebuilding what does not. title: We put a free, unlimited LLM inside a static web page — Transformers.js + a 135M model, zero servers
author: Astro
summary: Every LLM demo I have ever seen has the same fine print: bring your own API key , or the demo is rate-limited , or your prompts go to our server . So I built the opposite demo. Click "Load the model", wait for the one-time download, and chat. That's the whole signup flow. Honest limits It's a 135M-parameter model that lives in your RAM . The point isn't to replace an API; it's to show how far "the browser is the runtime" has come, and to give the LLM-curious a playground with literally zero setup and zero bill. title: Best AI Tool for Writing Notes in 2026: Three Scenarios, Three Clear Winners
author: Owais Khan
summary: Why Feature Lists Lie to You When You're Picking a Notes AI Every roundup of AI note-taking tools hands you the same checklist: summarization, transcription, search, collaboration. The problem is that two tools can both check every box and still be completely wrong for each other's users. The real question is not "does it have AI?" but "does its AI solve the specific friction I hit every single day?" The three scenarios below are drawn from documented user patterns in the sources — and in each one, a different tool wins for a reason that a feature matrix would never surface. Tool Starting paid price Key free tier Best for NoteGPT Not specified ("Save 30%" promo active) Free tier available Students, researchers, and creators who need multimedia summarization and full AI agent output Saner.AI $8/month (yearly) Free Starter plan Professionals, entrepreneurs, and ADHD users who need automatic task extraction and daily planning Notion Not specified in sources Free tier available Teams building structured knowledge bases and wikis Scenario 1 — The Student Drowning in Lectures, PDFs, and YouTube Explainers Picture a college student juggling recorded lectures, research PDFs, and YouTube videos for a single paper. She needs all of that material turned into usable notes — not just stored, but actually synthesized. This is the scenario where NoteGPT wins decisively, and the reason is architectural: NoteGPT is built as a full AI agent that routes tasks across GPT, Claude, Gemini, and DeepSeek to balance quality, speed, and cost. It does not just accept text — it summarizes YouTube videos, audio, and PDFs into what the product describes as "clear, in-depth visual insights," transcribes audio with speaker separation and timestamps while removing filler words, and can draft a document from outline to final draft iteratively. One interviewed student, Emily Johnson, described NoteGPT as transforming her study routine by summarizing lectures, making flashcards, and giving instant writing feedback — with a reported improvement in grades and exam confidence. Another student, Priya Sharma, called it her daily study companion for simplifying tough topics, summarizing recordings, and creating visuals. These are not edge-case power users; they represent the core student workflow the tool is explicitly designed for. NoteGPT reports 80 million-plus users worldwide and a 96% recommendation rate (based on a survey of 11,238 respondents), and claims users save an average of 2.6 hours daily (based on interviews with 500 users). For a student whose raw material is multimedia rather than typed text, no other tool in the sourced set matches this breadth. Scenario 2 — The Consultant Who Takes Notes but Never Acts on Them Here the situation flips. A freelance consultant attends four client calls a day, dumps rough notes into an app after each one, and then spends Sunday evening trying to reconstruct what she promised to whom. The bottleneck is not capture — it is conversion from note to action. Saner.AI is built precisely for this gap. Its AI assistant, Skai, automatically extracts to-dos from unstructured notes, generates scheduling suggestions around existing calendar meetings, and builds a daily focus plan without requiring manual input. The unified workspace covers notes, tasks, calendar, and email in one place, and the Chrome extension lets her save directly from the web mid-research. The pricing is also the most transparent of any tool in the sourced set: a genuinely usable free Starter plan, then $8/month on the yearly Standard plan, rising to $16/month yearly for the next tier. One verified user, Jerry, described Saner's Proactive AI as "the only AI-based tool that truly feels like a personal assistant" for managing constant email flow and multiple calendars. The Saner.AI source is candid about what the tool does not do — no Gantt charts, no complex task dependencies — which actually makes the recommendation cleaner: if your notes problem is really a task-conversion problem, Saner.AI is the right tool; if you need project timelines, it is not. The McKinsey Global Institute figure cited in the Saner.AI source is worth anchoring here: employees spend roughly 1.8 hours every day searching for information they already have. IDC puts that figure even higher, at around 2.5 hours per day, or 30% of the workday. A tool that automatically surfaces and schedules the right information attacks that loss directly in a way that a passive note store cannot. Scenario 3 — The Team That Outgrows a Personal Notes App Without Realizing It This is the edge case most buyers underestimate. A small team starts with one person's note system, it works, and then three more people join and suddenly nobody can find anything because the system was never designed for shared ownership. Notion is the sourced tool that handles this transition — it combines note-taking, project management, databases, wikis, and AI features in a single customizable workspace, with built-in Notion AI for writing, summarizing, brainstorming, and Q&A on shared content. Custom templates and layouts let teams standardize how information is captured across members. The honest caveat, stated directly in the Saner.AI source's own review of Notion: "you'll spend real time building the system before it works for you." That setup cost is real and it is the reason Notion is the wrong answer for a solo user who just wants to dump thoughts and have them organized automatically. But for a team that needs a shared knowledge base with consistent structure — the kind of thing a university lecturer like David Smith (an interviewed NoteGPT user) describes when he talks about creating lecture summaries, slides, and custom test questions for students — Notion's database and wiki layer provides governance that neither NoteGPT nor Saner.AI is designed to offer at team scale. The Zapier source, which tested over 50 note apps, lists Notion explicitly as its pick for collaboration, which corroborates this positioning from an independent testing perspective. The key disqualifier for teams is the same as the key qualifier: Notion requires deliberate system-building. If your team will invest that time, the payoff is a structured knowledge base that scales. If nobody wants to be the "Notion admin," the system collapses into chaos faster than a simpler tool would. The Single Thread Running Through All Three Verdicts Look at what actually drove each recommendation and a pattern emerges that no feature checklist captures: the winning tool in each scenario is the one whose AI operates at the right layer of the workflow. NoteGPT's AI operates at the input layer — it ingests multimedia, processes it through multiple models (GPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek), and produces structured output from raw, unstructured source material. That is exactly what a student needs when her inputs are videos and PDFs rather than typed text. Saner.AI's AI operates at the output layer — it takes notes that already exist and converts them into scheduled actions, reminders, and prioritized tasks. The AI's value is not in understanding the note itself but in understanding what the note implies you need to do next. That is the consultant's actual problem. Notion's AI operates at the organizational layer — it helps teams write, summarize, and query within a structure that humans have deliberately built. The AI amplifies a system; it does not replace the need to build one. That is appropriate for teams but a liability for individuals who want zero setup. Data security is worth noting for anyone handling sensitive client or research material: NoteGPT explicitly documents ISO 27001, SOC 2, GDPR, and CCPA compliance, states it does not sell or share personal data with third parties, does not use personal data for AI model training, and does not use hidden trackers or device fingerprinting. For researchers and consultants working with confidential information, that compliance stack matters and is worth verifying against whichever tool you choose. Match Your Situation to the Right Pick — and Stop Overthinking It If you recognized yourself in Scenario 1 — you are processing lectures, research papers, YouTube videos, or audio recordings and need them turned into usable written notes — choose NoteGPT. Its multi-model AI agent handles the full pipeline from raw multimedia to editable document, and its 96% recommendation rate across 11,238 surveyed users is the strongest satisfaction signal in the sourced set. If Scenario 2 is your life — you capture notes fine but they never become actions, your calendar is a mess, and you feel like you are constantly dropping balls — choose Saner.AI at $8/month on the yearly plan. The automatic daily planner and task extraction are the features that matter, and the free Starter plan lets you verify they work for your workflow before committing. If Scenario 3 describes your team — you have outgrown one person's system and need shared structure that multiple people can navigate — invest the setup time in Notion. Accept that the AI features are most valuable after the underlying database and wiki structure is in place, not before. The one scenario where none of these tools is obviously right: you want a graph-based personal knowledge system with maximum structural control. The Saner.AI source names Tana for that use case — high ceiling, high learning curve — and Capacities for researchers and writers who think in objects rather than pages. Both are documented in the sources but fall outside the mainstream writing-notes use case this comparison addresses. The default recommendation for most readers — students, solo professionals, and individual researchers — is NoteGPT if your notes start as multimedia, and Saner.AI if your notes start as text and need to become tasks. Those two tools solve genuinely different problems, and picking the wrong one means paying for AI that never fires at the moment you actually need it.
